patient.name: Walter Simmons
patient.chiefComplaint: Increasing shortness of breath over 2 days

history.hpi: Patient reports gradually worsening shortness of breath and productive cough with thicker, darker sputum over the past 2 days. Denies fever or chest pain. Has used his rescue inhaler more than usual with only partial relief. No recent travel, no known sick contacts. Lives alone, was able to walk to the door for EMS but stopped twice to catch his breath.
pastMedical: 40 pack-year smoking history, quit 3 years ago
history.events: Called EMS after rescue inhaler use provided only partial relief and breathing continued to worsen

scene.location: Single-story home, patient found seated in a recliner in the living room, oxygen concentrator nearby but not in use
scene.safety: No hazards to crew; cluttered living room, adequate access for stretcher
scene.bystanders: Patient lives alone; neighbor let crew in and is waiting outside
visualCues: Patient seated upright, leaning slightly forward
Home oxygen concentrator present but powered off
Cigarette-stained fingertips, though patient reports quitting 3 years ago
Empty albuterol MDI canister on side table

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 67-year-old male with known COPD seated upright in a recliner, mildly tachypneic with audible expiratory wheezing and pursed-lip breathing. He is alert and able to speak in full sentences with occasional pauses.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in full sentences with occasional pauses
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Mildly labored, prolonged expiratory phase, expiratory wheezing bilaterally
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and dry
otherFindings: Productive cough with thick, dark sputum
Able to speak in full sentences with brief pauses
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I just can't seem to catch my breath the last couple days."

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain history of onset, triggers, prior treatments, and full vital signs including SPO2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Onset of symptoms. Concurrent symptoms (e.g., fever, cough, rhinorrhea, tongue/lip swelling, rash, labored breathing, foreign body aspiration). Treatments prior to EMS: Oxygen, inhaler, nebulizer, other treatments, chronic or recent steroids. Full set of vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment), temperature, and O2 saturation
expectedActions.rationale: Establishes baseline severity and guides escalation decisions.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply nasal cannula oxygen titrated to 94-98% SPO2 (permissive hypoxia to 90% acceptable given COPD)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give supplemental oxygen for dyspnea to a target of 94–98% saturation. Escalate from a nasal cannula as needed to reach this goal
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia while avoiding over-oxygenation risk in chronic COPD.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

expectedActions.shortAction: Albuterol 5 mg nebulized with Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized (DuoNeb) for bronchospasm
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Albuterol 5 mg nebulized (or 6 puffs metered dose inhaler) should be administered to all patients in respiratory distress with signs of bronchospasm (e.g., known asthmatics, quiet wheezers). Repeat at this dose with unlimited frequency for ongoing respiratory distress. Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized should be given up to 3 doses in conjunction with albuterol
expectedActions.rationale: Bronchodilator and anticholinergic combination directly targets the bronchospasm driving the exacerbation.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

transitions.condition: Crew places patient on nasal cannula oxygen titrated toward 94-98% (permissive hypoxia acceptable per COPD history) and administers a nebulized bronchodilator treatment.
Crew delays or omits nebulized bronchodilator therapy despite clear signs of bronchospasm, allowing distress to progress.

phases.name: Oxygen and DuoNeb administered
phases.description: Crew applies nasal cannula oxygen and begins a nebulized albuterol/ipratropium (DuoNeb) treatment. Patient tolerates the treatment well without signs of severe distress requiring NIV escalation.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing bronchospasm from the wheezing, prolonged expiratory phase, and COPD history, the crew applies supplemental oxygen and initiates a nebulized bronchodilator treatment.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Mildly labored, wheezing improving with treatment
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and dry
otherFindings: Slightly improved air entry on auscultation

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs, SPO2, and work of breathing; document response to treatment
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Document key aspects of the exam at baseline and after each intervention: Respiratory rate. Oxygen saturation. Use of accessory muscles. Breath sounds and quality. Response to interventions
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms the treatment is working and guides transport decision.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

transitions.condition: Patient's work of breathing, wheezing, and SPO2 continue to improve with oxygen and nebulized bronchodilator therapy alone, without need for non-invasive ventilation.

phases.name: Symptoms improve without CPAP
phases.description: Patient's respiratory distress continues to improve with oxygen and nebulized bronchodilator therapy. Work of breathing decreases, wheezing diminishes, and SPO2 normalizes. Prepared for transport without need for CPAP.
phases.triggerCondition: Following oxygen and DuoNeb administration, the patient's wheezing and tachypnea steadily improve, confirming this is a mild exacerbation that does not require escalation to non-invasive ventilation.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and dry
otherFindings: Speaking in full sentences without pausing

phases.name: Bronchodilator therapy delayed
phases.description: Nebulized bronchodilator therapy is delayed despite clear bronchospasm findings. The patient's work of breathing and hypoxia progressively worsen, now showing early signs of a more severe exacerbation.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew focuses on oxygen application alone and delays starting nebulized DuoNeb despite audible wheezing and prolonged expiratory phase, allowing bronchospasm to worsen.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Increasingly labored, louder wheezing, speaking in shorter phrases
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and diaphoretic

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate DuoNeb without further delay: Albuterol 5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Albuterol 5 mg nebulized (or 6 puffs metered dose inhaler) should be administered to all patients in respiratory distress with signs of bronchospasm (e.g., known asthmatics, quiet wheezers). Repeat at this dose with unlimited frequency for ongoing respiratory distress. Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized should be given up to 3 doses in conjunction with albuterol
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed bronchodilator therapy allows a mild exacerbation to progress toward severe distress.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)
